papers.family: Contrastive UAV-view geo-localisation with auxiliary supervision (orientation pseudo-labels, rotation augmentation)
papers.contribution: Per the abstract only: an orientation-guided training framework that estimates UAV orientation relative to satellite imagery, trains a lightweight orientation-prediction module on pseudo-labels, and uses the labels for aligned satellite rotation augmentation. It claims state-of-the-art results on University-1652 and University-160k.
papers.mechanism: Hierarchical localisation yields pseudo-orientation labels. A lightweight module predicts orientation from contrastively learned embeddings and acts as an auxiliary training signal. The module is dropped at inference. Inference of mine: gains may come from augmentation and auxiliary supervision, not from any aggregation or negative-sampling change.
papers.limitations: Judged from the abstract alone, not a full read. The abstract does not say whether the negative-sampling regime is controlled, so it cannot separate orientation guidance from hard-negative effects. Its generality beyond UAV data is unknown. The pseudo-label quality is not described.
papers.evaluation: Claimed state of the art on University-1652 and University-160k. Ablations, baselines, variance and whether comparisons match in backbone and batch composition are not visible in the supplied evidence. Unverified.

papers.family: Contrastive learning with symmetric InfoNCE and hard-negative sampling (aggregation-free)
papers.contribution: Per the abstract: a simplified pipeline that drops aggregation modules and polar or other pre-processing. It introduces two hard-negative strategies: geographic-neighbour sampling, and sampling by embedding visual similarity. It claims state-of-the-art results on CVUSA, CVACT, University-1652 and VIGOR, plus better generalisation in cross-area settings.
papers.mechanism: Symmetric InfoNCE loss makes it easy to put hard negatives into the batch. The negatives come from geographic neighbours, which give a starting point, and from visual-similarity mining of embeddings. The abstract suggests this replaces the need for aggregation modules. Inference: the paper itself is a direct candidate for attributing gains to negative sampling instead of aggregation.
papers.limitations: Abstract only. The abstract does not show how much of the gain comes from the loss, the backbone or the sampling, nor whether aggregation-based baselines were rerun under the same sampling. Mining costs and the risk of false negatives are not discussed. 'Eliminates the need' is a claim that needs checking.
papers.evaluation: Reported on four common datasets, with a cross-area versus same-area comparison for generalisation. Ablation details, baseline fairness and variance are not in the evidence. Unverified.

papers.family: Unsupervised and semi-supervised cross-view geo-localisation via pseudo-labels
papers.contribution: Per the abstract: a framework for using unlabeled data in large-area ground-to-satellite CVGL, with a cross-view projection that gives initial pseudo-labels and a fast re-ranking step that refines them. It claims competitive performance against supervised methods on three benchmarks.
papers.mechanism: The projection gives initial pseudo-labels. Re-ranking uses a uniqueness assumption: a correctly paired ground-satellite image sits in a unique, identical scene. Inference: this uniqueness assumption could act as an implicit negative-selection mechanism, but the abstract does not say so.
papers.limitations: Abstract only. The uniqueness assumption may fail in repetitive scenes. Pseudo-label noise and the gap to fully supervised training are not quantified here. It does not address hard-negative sampling or aggregation directly, so its relevance to the research question is indirect.
papers.evaluation: Claims competitive results on three open-source benchmarks. The benchmark names, margins, ablations and variance are not in the evidence. Unverified.

papers.family: Aggregation-centred CVGL with foundation-model backbones
papers.contribution: Per the abstract: a DINOv2 backbone with a convolution adapter, a multi-scale channel reallocation module, and an aggregation module that adds Mixture-of-Experts routing for keys and values in cross-attention. It claims competitive results with fewer trained parameters on University-1652 and SUES-200.
papers.mechanism: Adapter fine-tuning adapts the backbone. Channel reallocation diversifies spatial features. MoE-routed cross-attention aggregation handles heterogeneous domains. Inference: several components change together, so any gain is confounded unless negative sampling and loss are held fixed.
papers.limitations: Abstract only. Three changes are bundled, so the contribution of aggregation alone cannot be isolated from the evidence. Training regime, loss and negative sampling are not stated. Claims are only 'competitive', not best. Coverage is limited to drone and satellite datasets.
papers.evaluation: Evaluated on University-1652 and SUES-200. Baselines, ablations, parameter counts and variance are not visible. Unverified. It is a useful aggregation-side comparator for the research question.

papers.family: Two-stage geo-localisation combining retrieval with relative pose estimation (fine-grained localisation)
papers.contribution: Per the abstract: PEnG, which first predicts the likely edge on a city-scale graph and then estimates relative pose within it for precise position. It argues sparse tiling caps accuracy. It also uses both viewpoints in the datasets (MVGL). It claims large gains, including a median error cut from 734 m to 22.77 m under 90° horizontal FOV.
papers.mechanism: Stage one is graph-edge retrieval. Stage two is relative pose estimation. The ensemble sets the final position. It targets the precision ceiling imposed by tile spacing, which is a different problem from embedding training.
papers.limitations: Abstract only. It addresses localisation granularity, not aggregation versus sampling, so it is largely off-axis for the research question. Dependence on a graph and on both views limits applicability. The settings behind the percentage figures are not described beyond the FOV.
papers.evaluation: Reports relative Top-5 m improvement of 213% and a 96.90% drop in median error. The dataset, baselines and protocol are not given in the evidence, so the figures are unverified and I did not check them.

opportunities.title: Factorial attribution of cross-view geo-localisation gains to negative sampling versus aggregation
opportunities.question: Does hard-negative sampling account for gains attributed to aggregation modules in cross-view geo-localisation, or do the two interact?
opportunities.hypothesis: Inference, not shown: under a fixed backbone, symmetric InfoNCE loss and batch size, an aggregation-based head and a no-aggregation head will differ less when both are trained with the same hard-negative regime (geographic-neighbour plus embedding-similarity mining) than when both are trained with random negatives. Falsified if the aggregation advantage over no aggregation is similar under random and hard-negative training, or if it is larger under hard-negative training.
opportunities.contribution: A controlled 2x2 (or 2x3) factorial study with aggregation (none vs MoE-routed cross-attention style) crossed with negative sampling (random, geographic-neighbour, similarity-mined). It would report interaction effects with seed variance and false-negative rates. The aim is attribution, not a new method.
opportunities.significance: If sampling explains most of the gain, reported aggregation improvements may reflect uncontrolled training differences. If the effects interact, aggregation is better understood as a compensator for weak training signals. Either result would inform how future CVGL papers set baselines.

assessments.summary: The question is relevant, but the evidence supports only a weak case. Everything here comes from abstracts, plus one metadata-only entry, and nothing was verified against full papers. Sample4Geo's abstract already argues, in purpose, that symmetric InfoNCE with hard negatives removes the need for aggregation modules. Its ablations may partly answer the question, and the abstract cannot confirm either way. The aggregation comparator (p-88d32985f8e9) bundles an adapter, channel reallocation and MoE routing, and its abstract reports only competitive results. It is a poor stand-in for an isolated aggregation arm. The 2x3 factorial design with seed variance and false-negative rates is not described in any supplied abstract. That is not proof of novelty, because only abstracts were read. This is a controlled-comparison study, not a new method, so its value depends on the rigor of its controls. Significance is plausible: if aggregation gains vanish under matched sampling, baseline practice in CVGL would change. Technical depth is modest. Generalization is uncertain, since the evidence covers University-1652 and SUES-200 for the aggregation arm and four datasets for Sample4Geo. Existing aggregation heads may be tied to losses and batch constructions that do not accept hard negatives easily. Sample4Geo's abstract says default losses make hard negatives difficult to include. That coupling could make the factorial design confounded or infeasible without retraining. The zero compute budget is a serious risk. It requires released code and checkpoints, and their availability is unverified. A null result may also be hard to publish at CVPR. No fatal prior-art overlap is shown, but it cannot be excluded either.
objections: Sample4Geo's ablations may already address sampling versus aggregation. Read the full paper before claiming a gap.
Novelty is uncertain and rests only on rigor of control. Absence of a matched ablation in abstracts is not evidence of novelty.
The aggregation arm is not isolated. The MoE-routed paper bundles three changes and states no sampling regime, so a clean aggregation-on/off comparison needs re-implementation.
Loss and sampling are coupled in the source work. Crossing aggregation with sampling under a fixed symmetric InfoNCE may favour the no-aggregation design by construction.
Zero compute budget makes the multi-seed 2x3 grid infeasible unless existing checkpoints can be reused, and no evidence shows they can.
Mining hard negatives risks false negatives in overlapping or neighbouring tiles. The design needs a way to measure or control this, and none is specified.
Results from University-1652 or SUES-200 may not transfer to ground-to-satellite datasets such as CVUSA, CVACT and VIGOR. Generalization is untested.

The interaction hypothesis is speculative. A null or backbone-dependent result would limit significance. ConGeo was seen only as metadata and the survey only as an abstract, so relevant controlled comparisons may be missed.

experiment.hypothesis: Inference, not shown: with backbone, symmetric InfoNCE loss, batch size, schedule and data fixed, the Recall@1 advantage of an aggregation head over a no-aggregation head (global pooling) is smaller under hard-negative training than under random-negative training. This implies sampling explains part of the gain attributed to aggregation.
datasets: University-1652 drone-to-satellite (primary; the only dataset shared by the supplied aggregation and sampling papers)
CVUSA or VIGOR same-area as an optional second dataset, only if time allows, to test transfer
baselines: No aggregation (pooled backbone embedding) with random negatives
No aggregation with geographic-neighbour plus similarity-mined hard negatives (the Sample4Geo-style regime)
Aggregation head (learnable-query cross-attention; MoE routing as an optional extra arm) with random negatives
Same aggregation head with hard negatives
If released checkpoints exist, their reported numbers are used only as a sanity check, not as arms
metrics: Recall@1 and AP on University-1652
Aggregation advantage per sampling regime: delta = R@1(agg) minus R@1(no agg), per seed
Interaction contrast: delta(random) minus delta(hard), with a paired bootstrap 95% CI over seeds
Estimated false-negative rate among mined negatives, using geographic overlap or ID duplication as a proxy
Trained-parameter count and wall-clock time per arm
experiment.config: 2x2 factorial: aggregation {none, learnable-query cross-attention} x negatives {random, hard-mined}. Backbone: one pretrained ViT or ConvNeXt, identical across arms, same input resolution, optimizer, LR schedule, epochs, batch size and augmentation. Loss: symmetric InfoNCE in every arm; the hard-negative arm only changes batch composition, with a warm-up on geographic neighbours and then embedding-similarity mining. Official University-1652 train/test split, with no tuning on test; hyperparameters are chosen once on a held-out validation slice of train locations and shared by all arms. 3 seeds (0, 1, 2) per arm, giving 12 runs. Reuse released code and checkpoints where licensed and available. Short-schedule training at reduced resolution is permitted, applied equally to all arms. Optional MoE arm: 1 seed only. Preregistered analysis: paired differences across seeds, no post hoc arm exclusion.
experiment.compute: Estimate, not measured: about 12 short runs at roughly 1-3 GPU-hours each, so about 1-2 days on one GPU. This exceeds the stated zero compute budget, so execution requires a researcher decision. A fallback is to reuse released checkpoints and rerun only the heads.
experiment.success: Hypothesis supported if the interaction contrast (delta under random minus delta under hard) is at least 2.0 R@1 points with the paired 95% bootstrap CI excluding 0, and the aggregation advantage under hard negatives is at most half of that under random negatives. Seed std of R@1 must be at most 0.7 points, otherwise the result is uninformative.
experiment.falsification: Falsified if |interaction contrast| is below 1.0 R@1 point, or its 95% CI includes 0 with the point estimate below 1.0, or if the aggregation advantage under hard negatives is at least 90% of the advantage under random negatives. Falsified in the opposite direction if the advantage is larger under hard negatives by more than 1.0 point (this would indicate synergy). Between 1.0 and 2.0 is inconclusive.
confounders: Sample4Geo's own ablations may already answer this question; the full paper must be read first (only abstracts were seen).
Loss and sampling are coupled in the source work, so the shared InfoNCE loss may favour no-aggregation by construction.
Aggregation head capacity and parameter count differ from the pooled baseline; control with a parameter-matched pooling-plus-MLP arm.
Hard-negative mining can introduce false negatives in overlapping or neighbouring tiles, which could depress the hard-negative arms.
Hyperparameters tuned for one regime may disadvantage another.
Only University-1652 is covered, so generalisation to ground-to-satellite datasets is untested.
Small seed count gives wide intervals.
Released code or checkpoints may be unavailable, which would force re-implementation.

papers.contribution: Per the abstract: a simplified pipeline that drops aggregation modules and polar or other pre-processing. papers.mechanism: Symmetric InfoNCE loss makes it easy to put hard negatives into the batch. papers.family: Contrastive UAV-view geo-localisation with auxiliary supervision (orientation pseudo-labels, rotation augmentation)
papers.contribution: Per the abstract only: an orientation-guided training framework that estimates UAV orientation relative to satellite imagery, trains a lightweight orientation-prediction module on pseudo-labels, and uses the labels for aligned satellite rotation augmentation. It claims state-of-the-art results on University-1652 and University-160k.
papers.mechanism: Hierarchical localisation yields pseudo-orientation labels. A lightweight module predicts orientation from contrastively learned embeddings and acts as an auxiliary training signal. The module is dropped at inference. Inference of mine: gains may come from augmentation and auxiliary supervision, not from any aggregation or negative-sampling change.
papers.limitations: Judged from the abstract alone, not a full read. The abstract does not say whether the negative-sampling regime is controlled, so it cannot separate orientation guidance from hard-negative effects. Its generality beyond UAV data is unknown. The pseudo-label quality is not described.
papers.evaluation: Claimed state of the art on University-1652 and University-160k. Ablations, baselines, variance and whether comparisons match in backbone and batch composition are not visible in the supplied evidence. Unverified.

papers.family: Contrastive learning with symmetric InfoNCE and hard-negative sampling (aggregation-free)
papers.contribution: Per the abstract: a simplified pipeline that drops aggregation modules and polar or other pre-processing. It introduces two hard-negative strategies: geographic-neighbour sampling, and sampling by embedding visual similarity. It claims state-of-the-art results on CVUSA, CVACT, University-1652 and VIGOR, plus better generalisation in cross-area settings.
papers.mechanism: Symmetric InfoNCE loss makes it easy to put hard negatives into the batch. The negatives come from geographic neighbours, which give a starting point, and from visual-similarity mining of embeddings. The abstract suggests this replaces the need for aggregation modules. Inference: the paper itself is a direct candidate for attributing gains to negative sampling instead of aggregation.
papers.limitations: Abstract only. The abstract does not show how much of the gain comes from the loss, the backbone or the sampling, nor whether aggregation-based baselines were rerun under the same sampling. Mining costs and the risk of false negatives are not discussed. 'Eliminates the need' is a claim that needs checking.
papers.evaluation: Reported on four common datasets, with a cross-area versus same-area comparison for generalisation. Ablation details, baseline fairness and variance are not in the evidence. Unverified.

papers.family: Unsupervised and semi-supervised cross-view geo-localisation via pseudo-labels
papers.contribution: Per the abstract: a framework for using unlabeled data in large-area ground-to-satellite CVGL, with a cross-view projection that gives initial pseudo-labels and a fast re-ranking step that refines them. It claims competitive performance against supervised methods on three benchmarks.
papers.mechanism: The projection gives initial pseudo-labels. Re-ranking uses a uniqueness assumption: a correctly paired ground-satellite image sits in a unique, identical scene. Inference: this uniqueness assumption could act as an implicit negative-selection mechanism, but the abstract does not say so.
papers.limitations: Abstract only. The uniqueness assumption may fail in repetitive scenes. Pseudo-label noise and the gap to fully supervised training are not quantified here. It does not address hard-negative sampling or aggregation directly, so its relevance to the research question is indirect.
papers.evaluation: Claims competitive results on three open-source benchmarks. The benchmark names, margins, ablations and variance are not in the evidence. Unverified.

papers.family: Aggregation-centred CVGL with foundation-model backbones
papers.contribution: Per the abstract: a DINOv2 backbone with a convolution adapter, a multi-scale channel reallocation module, and an aggregation module that adds Mixture-of-Experts routing for keys and values in cross-attention. It claims competitive results with fewer trained parameters on University-1652 and SUES-200.
papers.mechanism: Adapter fine-tuning adapts the backbone. Channel reallocation diversifies spatial features. MoE-routed cross-attention aggregation handles heterogeneous domains. Inference: several components change together, so any gain is confounded unless negative sampling and loss are held fixed.
papers.limitations: Abstract only. Three changes are bundled, so the contribution of aggregation alone cannot be isolated from the evidence. Training regime, loss and negative sampling are not stated. Claims are only 'competitive', not best. Coverage is limited to drone and satellite datasets.
papers.evaluation: Evaluated on University-1652 and SUES-200. Baselines, ablations, parameter counts and variance are not visible. Unverified. It is a useful aggregation-side comparator for the research question.

papers.family: Two-stage geo-localisation combining retrieval with relative pose estimation (fine-grained localisation)
papers.contribution: Per the abstract: PEnG, which first predicts the likely edge on a city-scale graph and then estimates relative pose within it for precise position. opportunities.title: Factorial attribution of cross-view geo-localisation gains to negative sampling versus aggregation
opportunities.question: Does hard-negative sampling account for gains attributed to aggregation modules in cross-view geo-localisation, or do the two interact?
opportunities.hypothesis: Inference, not shown: under a fixed backbone, symmetric InfoNCE loss and batch size, an aggregation-based head and a no-aggregation head will differ less when both are trained with the same hard-negative regime (geographic-neighbour plus embedding-similarity mining) than when both are trained with random negatives. Falsified if the aggregation advantage over no aggregation is similar under random and hard-negative training, or if it is larger under hard-negative training.
opportunities.contribution: A controlled 2x2 (or 2x3) factorial study with aggregation (none vs MoE-routed cross-attention style) crossed with negative sampling (random, geographic-neighbour, similarity-mined). It would report interaction effects with seed variance and false-negative rates. The aim is attribution, not a new method.
opportunities.significance: If sampling explains most of the gain, reported aggregation improvements may reflect uncontrolled training differences. If the effects interact, aggregation is better understood as a compensator for weak training signals. Either result would inform how future CVGL papers set baselines.
